themes.name: Nobody Can Verify Downstream
themes.plain: Once data or an instruction leaves your own systems, you cannot look inside the partner, ad platform, or trained model that receives it. So compliance and safety can only be guessed at from the outside, never proven.
themes.evidence: All three models said proving downstream consent, deletion and purpose enforcement is blocked by opaque ad platforms, agency segments and models that cannot unlearn, and the same opacity showed up as vendors exposing no agent identity in safe, auditable agent execution and as agents that can simply lie about being human in distinguishing and governing agentic traffic.

themes.name: Start From What Already Failed
themes.plain: Every model opens the same way: go dig up cases your organization already decided or already logged, and turn them into labels, rules, or code. Nobody starts by designing the ideal system.
themes.evidence: Models proposed reconstructing data exits from network and vendor logs rather than asking teams, tracing one real opt-out end to end in provable downstream consent, deletion and purpose enforcement, mining rejected content in governance and review of generative marketing content at volume, reading the actual SQL behind every definition of customer in the governed semantic context layer, and labeling sessions where an agent was already known in distinguishing and governing agentic traffic.

themes.name: Chokepoint Before Trust
themes.plain: When the models cannot trust what is acting or where data goes, they route everything through one door they own. Put a gateway in front of every write, log it, cap it, and make permissions expire, because a sent message or a spent budget cannot be taken back.
themes.evidence: All three models put a proxy or single gateway with hard limits and a kill switch in front of agent writes in safe, auditable agent execution, and in provable downstream consent, deletion and purpose enforcement one model replaced perpetual audience lists with short-lived cohorts that expire unless consent is refreshed.

themes.name: Agents Break Web Assumptions
themes.plain: Software agents now browse, buy, and act for people, but the systems underneath were built for humans clicking pages. The stack cannot tell who is on the other end, what they may do, or what a term in their request even means.
themes.evidence: Distinguishing and governing agentic traffic and safe, auditable agent execution both turn on missing agent identity and unreliable self-declaration, and the governed semantic context layer exists because agents need machine-readable definitions the current tools never had to provide.

themes.name: Incentives, Not Architecture
themes.plain: Some of these are not engineering problems at all. Different teams inside the company, and outside partners, gain from keeping their own answer or staying opaque, so no schema or protocol can settle the dispute for them.
themes.evidence: Models called semantic consensus in the governed semantic context layer a political problem about who owns the number, said agent operators in distinguishing and governing agentic traffic have nothing to lose by lying, and described ad platforms in provable downstream consent, deletion and purpose enforcement as structurally rewarded for being black boxes.
